summary: Bob Thomas's comments on John Day's File Access Protocol proposal in RFC 520. He thinks a protocol of that kind is a good idea, sees its commands as generic file system calls, and suggests mostly additions such as an append mode for opening files.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC comments on the File Access Protocol proposed in RFC 520. It suggests additions so remote programs can use files in ways available to local programs.

subtitle: Suggestions for extending the proposed File Access Protocol.

tldr.problem: The proposed File Access Protocol aimed to make remote file operations available to programs, but the RFC identifies missing capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: Bob Thomas suggests append mode, a way to locate used blocks, file status information, file handles, and control over local transformations.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a set of proposed additions to RFC 520, not a revised protocol specification.

sections.title: Extending Remote File Access
sections.content:
Bob Thomas calls the File Access Protocol proposed in RFC 520 a good idea. He describes FTP as supporting file activity typically initiated by a user, while FAP aims to support operating-system-level file operations through a remote server.

His comments propose additions intended to make more local file capabilities available remotely.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP transfers files, while FAP aims to let programs make file-system requests remotely. Thomas supports the idea and suggests features for the proposal.

sections.title: Append Mode and File Information
sections.content:
Thomas proposes an OPEN mode A for append, which he describes as equivalent in file-pointer action to opening for writing and setting the pointer to the end. He also proposes FNUB, a command to find the next used block, so a remote user could navigate a file with holes.

He lists useful file information such as access rights, size, access dates, and page-level access controls.
sections.plainLanguage: An append mode would let a user add data at the end of a file. A proposed FNUB command would help locate the next used block in a file with gaps.

sections.title: Multiple Files and Transformations
sections.content:
The proposed protocol did not support access to several files at once. Thomas suggests server-chosen file handles so later commands can identify which open file they refer to.

He also says a remote user should be able to suppress local file transformations when direct access to the stored data is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: File handles could let a remote program work with several open files. The user should also be able to request data without local transformations.

references.text: Day, J. D., "File Access Protocol", RFC 520.
